Design

The primary benchmark compares four processes whose population logarithmic significand (U={_{10}X}) is exactly uniform on ([0,1)). In v2, the latent-regime construction uses exactly half of the sequences in each conditional regime. This removes finite-sample noise from a randomly realized mixture weight and isolates the aggregation mechanism itself. A separate experiment below restores random sequence-level composition.

Code 
design_table <- make_design_table(
  n_seq = params$n_seq,
  seq_len = params$seq_len,
  rho = params$rho,
  theta = params$theta
)

Finite-sample behavior of the standard iid test

The dashed line below is the conventional 5% critical value of a (^2_8) reference law. The population first-digit probabilities are nevertheless exactly Benford in every construction. In the latent control, the number of sequences in the two non-Benford conditional regimes is fixed at exactly 50/50. Differences in rejection behavior therefore cannot be attributed to random fluctuations in the realized mixture weight.

Code 
p_chi <- plot_chisq_distribution(primary)
p_chi
ggplot2::ggsave(
  file.path(fig_dir, "figure_chisq_sampling.pdf"),
  p_chi, width = 8, height = 5
)

Sequence information

We use the complex first circular transition moment

[ m_1= {s,t}{2i(U{s,t+1}-U_{s,t})}. ]

Rather than estimating a shuffle baseline by repeated permutations, the code subtracts its exact conditional expectation under a random permutation within each sequence. For a sequence of length (L), with (z_j=(2iU_j)), that expectation is

[ . ]

This is computationally much cheaper and, importantly, removes the apparent transition coherence generated solely by persistent latent composition within a sequence.

Code 
p_trans <- plot_transition_coherence(primary)
p_trans
ggplot2::ggsave(

)

Analytical check for the mean Pearson statistic

Because the population first-digit probabilities are known exactly, the expected Pearson statistic can also be computed from the within-sequence covariance structure. For the wrapped-Gaussian process the covariance is obtained from the Fourier coefficients of the digit intervals; for the rotation it is obtained from exact circular interval overlaps; and for the balanced latent mixture it follows from stratified multinomial variation. This gives a direct theory-versus-simulation check rather than relying on Monte Carlo alone.

Code 
chisq_theory <- make_chisq_theory_table(
  primary, rho = params$rho, theta = params$theta, seq_len = params$seq_len
)

Design-aware calibration of the same Pearson discrepancy

The classical Pearson statistic is kept fixed; what changes is its reference law. Let (p_8) denote the first eight empirical digit proportions and let (p_8) denote their Benford targets. With the ninth cell determined by the unit-sum constraint,

[ X_n^2 = n(p_8-p_8)^ A (p_8-p_8), A=(p_1{-1},,p_8{-1})+p_9^{-1}^. ]

The independent sequences provide a direct estimate of (={n(p_8-p_8)}). For equal sequence length (L), this is (L) times the covariance of the sequence-level digit proportions. In the exactly balanced latent design we estimate covariance within latent strata and combine it using the fixed 50/50 design weights; otherwise random composition would incorrectly be treated as part of the sampling design that was fixed by construction.

If (_1,,_8) are the eigenvalues of (A^{1/2}A^{1/2}), the iid multinomial reference corresponds to (_j=1) for all (j). We report three design-aware calibrations:

  1. a first-order design-effect correction, dividing (X_n^2) by ();
  2. a second-order Satterthwaite/Rao–Scott-style correction, [ a=, =, X_n2/a  2_; ]
  3. a sequence-aware Wald statistic using () directly.

The point is not to claim a universal Benford correction. These procedures are valid only to the extent that the declared independent-sequence structure is the relevant observation design. They provide a constructive check of the paper’s central claim: when the design is retained, the same discrepancy can be calibrated against the appropriate sampling variability rather than against an iid multinomial law.

The signed effect is (2,-1). Its sign records ordering; its magnitude records univariate separation across Monte Carlo replications.

Conditioning reveals the latent-regime construction

The latent model uses (UZ=0(2,1)) and (UZ=1(1,2)). In the primary v2 benchmark, exactly half of the sequences are assigned to each regime. Neither conditional law is Benford, while the corresponding equal-weight pooled population is exactly uniform.

Code 
p_mix <- plot_latent_mixture(representative$mixture)
p_mix
ggplot2::ggsave(
  file.path(fig_dir, "figure_latent_mixture.pdf"),
  p_mix, width = 9, height = 4
)

Random cluster composition as a separate observation-design effect

The balanced latent control isolates aggregation from a second effect that appeared in the first numerical version. If sequence-level regimes are instead drawn independently,

[ Z_s(1/2), ]

the superpopulation mixture remains exactly Benford, but a realized dataset contains a random fraction () of the two regimes. Conditional on that realized composition, the pooled density is

[ f(u) =,2u+(1-),2(1-u) =1+2(/2)(2u-1). ]

Thus a conventional iid Benford test can react strongly to random cluster composition even though the population mixing mechanism itself has exactly equal weights. We keep this effect out of the primary benchmark and study it separately here.

Sensitivity to stochastic dependence

For the wrapped-Gaussian random walk, the first circular Fourier coefficient of the innovation kernel is parameterized as

[ =(-222). ]

Changing () therefore changes dependence while leaving the population Benford marginal exactly unchanged.

Pass 3A: Does the result depend on the choice n = 100,000?

The primary benchmark intentionally uses a large sample so that the iid Pearson reference is not compromised by sparse expected cells. A legitimate concern is that the calibration effect might therefore be an artifact of that particular choice. We separate three quantities: the number of independent sequences (B), their length (L), and the total number of records (n=BL).

Two complementary grids are used for the wrapped-Gaussian circular Markov construction at (). In the first, (B=400) is fixed and (L) varies, so total sample size changes while the number of independent sampling units does not. In the second, (n=100{,}000) is fixed while (B) and (L) trade off. This distinguishes a large-(n) effect from a cluster-length/design effect.

Pass 3B: A continuous-significand goodness-of-fit statistic

Pearson’s statistic uses only the nine first-digit cells. To check that the calibration issue is not tied to this discretization, we also use a Cramér–von Mises statistic for the continuous log-significand distribution,

[ W_n2=n_01{F_n(u)-u}^2,du. ]

The code evaluates the integral on a fixed interior grid. Under iid Uniform sampling, the standard asymptotic 5% critical value is approximately 0.461. For design-aware calibration, the covariance of the sequence-level empirical CDF is estimated on the same grid. The resulting quadratic form again has a weighted-chi-square limit, so we use the same second-order moment-matching principle as for Pearson. This is an intentionally simple check of generality, not a claim that this discretized implementation is an optimal CvM procedure.

Pass 3C: Level and power under a genuine marginal alternative

The previous experiments keep the Benford marginal exactly correct and study size. To show that design correction is not synonymous with discarding marginal information, we also introduce a smooth one-parameter departure from uniformity,

[ f_(u)=1+(2u-1),. ]

Its CDF is (F_(u)=(1-)u+u^2). We generate the same () circular Markov process on a latent uniform scale and apply (F_^{-1}) pointwise. Thus () is exactly the dependent Benford null, while (>0) changes the one-time marginal without changing the underlying latent sequence construction. The experiment compares the inflated iid references with the design-aware Pearson and CvM procedures.

Code

    progress = TRUE
  )
  saveRDS(pass3_power, pass3_power_file)
} else {
  pass3_power <- readRDS(pass3_power_file)
}

A positive control for the information-boundary discussion

The significand-preserving order shift later in the document is an impossibility construction: by definition it leaves every log-significand unchanged. To avoid suggesting that digit analysis is never informative, we add a deliberately simple positive control. A small amount of round-number heaping moves observations toward powers of ten and hence changes the log-significand distribution. The same digit statistics that are exactly blind to integer-order magnitude shifts react strongly when the observed representation itself changes.

Code 
if (isTRUE(params$recompute_pass3) || !file.exists(pass3_boundary_file)) {
  pass3_boundary <- run_manipulation_boundary_demo(
    n_seq = params$n_seq,
    seq_len = params$seq_len,
    seed = SEED_PASS3_BOUNDARY
  )
  saveRDS(pass3_boundary, pass3_boundary_file)
} else {
  pass3_boundary <- readRDS(pass3_boundary_file)
}

significand-preserving magnitude shift 8.881531 0.352388 0.078359 0.000055
round-number heaping 117.615305 0.000000 14.676449 0.002220

A game-theoretic route to Benford

Morrison’s multiplication game provides a substantively different route to the same logarithmic invariant distribution. Players choose significands in ([1,10)); after taking base-10 logarithms, multiplication modulo powers of ten becomes addition on the circle. If one player uses Haar measure, equivalently the Benford distribution on significands, the product state is uniform modulo one regardless of the other player’s action.

We use the winning set

[ W=[0,_{10}4), ]

so Player 1 wins when the product significand begins with 1, 2, or 3. Its game value under Haar measure is ((W)=_{10}4).

Static multiplication game

The heatmap compares several mixed strategies on the log scale. The Haar row and Haar column should be flat at the game value: if either player uses Haar randomization, the other player cannot move the expected payoff away from (_{10}4).

One-step strategic washout

The next experiment is an elementary dynamic extension, not a claim about equilibrium learning. The initial state is deliberately non-Benford and Player 2 uses a deterministic, state-dependent response. Player 1 then draws a fresh Haar log-action. Translation invariance implies that the next state is exactly uniform conditional on the entire past and on Player 2’s response.

Code 
if (isTRUE(params$recompute) || !file.exists(game_washout_file)) {
  game_washout <- run_strategic_washout(n = params$game_washout_n, seed = SEED_GAME_WASHOUT)
  saveRDS(game_washout, game_washout_file)
} else {
  game_washout <- readRDS(game_washout_file)
}

Repeated non-Haar play can still mix toward Benford

Finally, both players use fixed, concentrated wrapped-normal mixed strategies on the log scale. Neither action distribution is Haar. Their sum is nevertheless a non-lattice random increment on the circle, and repeated convolution drives the state toward Haar measure. For wrapped-normal actions with standard deviations (_A) and (_B), the magnitude of the first Fourier coefficient decays exactly at rate

[ ^t, ={-22(_A2+_B^2)}. ]

This experiment is included as a mechanism illustration: Benford can describe the induced long-run state even though neither player’s mixed strategy is itself Benford.

Code 
if (isTRUE(params$recompute) || !file.exists(game_mixing_file)) {

    seed = SEED_GAME_MIXING
  )
  saveRDS(game_mixing, game_mixing_file)
} else {

}

Significand-preserving manipulation

This experiment is deliberately an identification example rather than a realistic model of a particular fraud scheme. Starting from

[ X_t=10^{K_t+U_t}, ]

we independently flag a fraction (q) of observations and shift their order of magnitude by an integer amount:

[ X_t’=10^{K_t+_t+U_t}. ]

The entire significant-digit sequence is therefore unchanged observation by observation.

Code 
if (isTRUE(params$recompute) || !file.exists(manipulation_file)) {
  manipulation <- run_manipulation_experiment(
    n = params$n_seq * params$seq_len,
    q = params$manipulation_q,
    shift_orders = params$manipulation_shift_orders,
    K_fourier = params$K_fourier,
    seed = SEED_MANIPULATION
  )
  saveRDS(manipulation, manipulation_file)
} else {
  manipulation <- readRDS(manipulation_file)
}

stopifnot(isTRUE(manipulation$exact_u_identity))

manip_names <- c(chisq = "chi-square", cvm = "CvM", B_K = "B(K)")
manip_table <- data.frame(
  statistic = unname(manip_names[names(manipulation$before)]),
  original = as.numeric(manipulation$before),
  manipulated = as.numeric(manipulation$after),
  difference = as.numeric(manipulation$after - manipulation$before)
)
